# Come, Eat of My Bread: Making Passage Across Life's Thresholds

When faith formation is viewed as a journey, we begin to see the importance of helping people cross major life milestones—making passage across life's nodal thresholds. Life is a sojourn of stages demarcated by junctures, crossroads, landmarks, and way-stations that mark the way. Wisdom literature, especially Proverbs, meaningfully depicts faith formation as a rite of passage for those on the journey of life. Proverbs summons the humble and receptive to make passage into wisdom. Effectively, faith formation in the fear of God involves marking milestones of life and faith development, helping pilgrims get onto the paths of righteousness, make progress toward wisdom, and eventually become initiated into her. In this way, we serve well ourselves, our families, and our churches by understanding how rites of passage and faith formation.

On one level, Proverbs 1-9 can be understood as an urgent appeal (through ten lectures) for the simple, youthful, and naive to embrace wisdom. But the initial appeals to embrace wisdom in Proverbs 1-7 climax in Proverbs 8-9 with a picture of wisdom building a house that one is to inhabit and laying out a table at which one is to feast. Solomon is not merely aiming to teach his son about wisdom; he is earnest to initiate his son into wisdom—to forsake the wayward harlot of foolishness and to betroth the unparalleled beauty of wisdom. In this way, the first nine chapters of this collection of wisdom sayings—and the book as a whole—can be seen through the lens of a rite of passage: an invitation to leave behind an old season of life—youth, naivete, evil, and foolishness—to enter into a new life of responsibility and discretion, and to be incorporated into the faith community with a whole new status.

In the context of Proverbs, the invitation for the youth to cross the threshold into wisdom comes from the father, the mother, the faith community, and Lady Wisdom. The appeal of the father and mother punctuate the text, inviting the son to embrace wisdom (1:8-10, 15; 2:1-5; 3:1-4, 11-12, 21; 4:1-2, 10, 20; 5:1-2, 7; 6:1-3, 20-22; 7:1-5; 8:32). Wisdom itself is personified as a beautiful woman who is to be loved, cherished, and adored (1:20-33; 8:1-36; 9:1-12). In this section, Lady Wisdom is contrasted to Dame Folly, an anti-wisdom figure depicted as a forbidden and strange woman (5:1-23; 6:20-35; 7:1-27; 9:13-18). Certainly, the appearances of the wayward woman are a warning against lust, adultery, and sexual sin. But this character serves a larger purpose, representing the death-trap of a foolish life. To be initiated into the wrong way of life is like falling prey to a seductress—one becomes a lamb to the slaughter, a victim culpable of his own death sentence. In Proverbs 1-9, the loud and beautiful voice of wisdom is the choice alternative voice to boisterous and lewd voice of folly and evil. Both are seeking to initiate the youth, forming him into a certain kind of man. Wisdom makes an appeal for the youth to betrothed to her, turning him into a righteous man of royal quality. Folly hunts the youth to degrade, destroy, and devour him, leading him on the paths of death and self-demise.

Proverbs also depicts negative rites of passage—initiations into wickedness. The gang entices the youth to join—cross over into—their greedy and homicidal ranks (1:8-19). Once they join the criminal band, they seal their own deadly fate. Wicked men "leave the straight paths" (2:13) for crooked, perverse, and devious ways (2:12-16). These evil men seek to allure youth into "the way of evil" (2:11). The forbidden, strange woman seduces the youth to "go to her" (2:19) and abandon the paths of life (2:16-19; 5:1-14; 6:20-35; 7:1-27). She wanders onto the streets (7:12), she lurks at corners (7:12), she meets her naive prey outside (7:10-11), ensnaring the simple who stand at a crossroads (7:8). Like a predator, she targets the simple and naive (7:6-9). She lures these untrained and immature youth to leave the road (7:25), stray onto her paths (7:25), and enter her home (5:8; 7:19-20, 27). Inasmuch as a rite of passage involve crossing life's thresholds, these deceived youth quite literally cross over the threshold of a door (5:8) into the deadly vice and vile voluptuousness. But her paths and her house sink down to death (5:5-6; 7:18-19, 26-27); those who enter in with her go down to destruction with her. Godless initiation by the gang, evil men, or the forbidden woman each presents a warring rival to godly rites of passage. To be initiated into these evil ways is self-ambush, self-destruction, self-demise, self-treason, and self-condemnation (1:18-19, 31-32; 6:27-29, 32; 7:22-23; cf. 1:26-27).

While we consider initiating our youth into wisdom, righteousness, mature adulthood, and Christian living, we must be aware of rival rites of passage. Through media, entertainment, and education, culture's agenda is to initiate youth into a way of worldly thinking and living. There is a grand spiritual conflict at work—a spiritual battle raging for the lives of the youth. The world seeks to lure, entice, seduce youth to join the ranks of godlessness. Once youth are initiated, they are captured as in a deadly snare. Formation is wisdom combats the allurements of folly with the captivating beauty of wisdom that leads to moral transformation. But moral development is much more than measuring the goodness or badness of conduct. We must aim to initiate youth into a wise life that leads to deep transformation: establishing beliefs, reforming conduct, purifying motivations, sanctifying imagination, building worldview, fortifying relationships, and inculcating virtue. To this end, we allow Proverbs to help shape our approach to formation—a spiritual pedagogy—that grounds us with a biblical perspective on how we grow, mature, and change.

## Key Ideas

- Rites of passage mark major milestones of life and faith by helping people cross thresholds—make passage across—various seasons of life.
- Liminality is a borderland space—a demarcation of two spheres—which summons one to cross into a new status and social standing in the community.
- Rites of passage aim to initiate and involve establishing boundaries, overcoming ordeals, elucidating progress, inaugurating new seasons, incorporating into a community with a new status.
- The world has rival rites of passage that seek to initiate youth into wickedness; Christians must combat these negative rites of passage with godly rites of passage.

## Reflection Questions

<Question id="Pro-Ses5-RefQue-1">1. Did you have any help in navigating the major milestones of your life and faith? What was your experience like as you went through major transitions in life and discipleship?</Question>
<Question id="Pro-Ses5-RefQue-2">2. Why might it be important for Christian families and church communities to take this process seriously? What are the consequences if we do not help people navigate the major transitions of life?</Question>
<Question id="Pro-Ses5-RefQue-3">3. What are major milestones in life and faith? How would you describe the transition from one phase to another?</Question>
<Question id="Pro-Ses5-RefQue-4">4. What are key characteristics of a right of passage? How might we approach rites of passage from a distinctively Christian perspective? How does the book of Proverbs assist us in this work?</Question>
